No news has been published yet.
SITE_EN.Dron, kt\u00f3remu misj\u0119 zlecasz s\: A drone you can task with words
SITE_EN.Badamy, jak modele j\u0119zykowo-wizyjne: We study how vision-language models (VLMs) control a real drone and use reasoning to find and recognise targets.
SITE_EN.Modele j\u0119zykowe potrafi\u0105 ju\u0: Language models can already do almost anything, so we are exploring how they handle drone navigation, particularly in unfamiliar terrain. FlySearch builds on research co-authored by our academic supervisor, Marek Cygan, which studied language-model control of drones in simulated search-and-rescue missions. We are taking that research into the real world.
SITE_EN.Projekt sprawdza, jak modele j\u0119zyko: The project explores how language models understand space and how simulation results transfer to real environments. We work on two fronts. We train the model in Unreal Engine using 3D terrain models reconstructed with Gaussian Splatting. At the same time, we test it on a real drone whose onboard computer connects to the model through our API over a cellular network. The model receives a task description, the target object and the search area boundaries. The process then repeats: the drone sends an image and its altitude, the model analyses the scene and returns its reasoning and a proposed movement, and the drone carries it out.
SITE_EN.Misj\u0119 mo\u017cna zleci\u0107 zwyk\u: Missions can be described in ordinary language, allowing even someone unfamiliar with drone control to prepare and run them. This is particularly promising for finding people and objects in the field.
SITE_EN.Hubert Zientara, Jan Miko\u0142ajczyk i: Hubert Zientara, Jan Mikołajczyk and Jan Matusiak with the FlyLLM poster at ML in PL 2026.
SITE_EN.Mamy dzia\u0142aj\u0105cy system. Dron z: We have a working system. A drone with an onboard computer connects to the model through our API over a cellular network, sends images and altitude, and then executes the movements selected by the model. We train the model through reinforcement learning in 3D reconstructions of real places created with Gaussian Splatting. Our fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B model achieved a 51.72% success rate on the FlySearch FS-1 benchmark (60.88% in forests and 42.55% in urban environments), an improvement of 22.41 percentage points over the base model. We presented these results in “FlyLLM: training VLMs with RL in Gaussian-splat environments to explore 3D spaces and navigate in the real world” at ML in PL 2026. The final real-world testing campaign is under way.
SITE_EN.Celem jest opublikowanie wraz z zespo\u0: Our goal is to publish a research paper with the team showing how vision-language models perform on a real drone and how simulation results transfer to the real world. The next step is to complete the testing campaign and analyse its results.
SITE_EN.Pseudosatelita, kt\u00f3ry wraca na ziem: A pseudo-satellite that returns to Earth
SITE_EN.Budujemy stratosferycznego drona typu HA: We are building a stratospheric HAPS drone. A weather balloon carries it aloft, it measures atmospheric conditions in the stratosphere, and then it returns to Earth autonomously. It flies higher than conventional drones and costs less than a satellite.
SITE_EN.Hawk Eye to pseudosatelita, czyli HAPS (: Hawk Eye is a pseudo-satellite, or HAPS (High Altitude Platform Station): an unmanned platform operating in the stratosphere. Today, atmospheric profiles are mostly measured using disposable radiosondes that are lost after each launch. Our drone returns to Earth after collecting measurements and can fly again, significantly reducing the cost of daily meteorological data collection. It is also much cheaper than a satellite.
SITE_EN.Balon meteorologiczny wynosi drona na wy: A weather balloon carries the drone to an altitude of 20–25 km. During ascent, its sensors collect an atmospheric profile. After separating from the balloon, the drone performs an autonomous, controlled return flight. Airframe design is crucial: a large wingspan provides controllability in the thin air. The wings are treated with anti-icing coatings, while the electronics handle navigation, autopilot functions and communication.
SITE_EN.Platforma mo\u017ce zast\u0105pi\u0107 j: The platform could replace disposable radiosondes in daily atmospheric profiling, support critical infrastructure monitoring and help detect the effects of natural disasters early. Potential users include weather services, scientific institutions, infrastructure operators and emergency management teams.
SITE_EN.Zesp\u00f3\u0142 Hawk Eye z pierwszym p\: The Hawk Eye team with its first airframe, with a wingspan of 3 m.
SITE_EN.Zbudowali\u015bmy pierwszy p\u0142atowie: We have built our first airframe with a 3 m wingspan and are flight-testing its electronics, autonomous control and anti-icing coatings. Flights so far have been successful. We tested the measurement electronics gondola in a cryogenic wind tunnel at −30°C: the power supply worked reliably, the sensors returned correct readings and the balloon release system worked in all three trials. A second airframe prototype is under construction.
SITE_EN.Celem jest w pe\u0142ni autonomiczna pla: Our goal is a fully autonomous HAPS platform that takes measurements in the stratosphere after balloon launch, uses photovoltaic panels to stay airborne for as long as possible, and returns safely to Earth. The next step is a stratospheric gondola flight to test the electronics, communication range and atmospheric profiling. In parallel, we are building the next airframe and the autonomous flight system.

researchHtml.pl:
Research

Gaussian Splatting

Niesamowita metoda, która pozwala tworzyć modele 3D całych scen z zaledwie kilku zdjęć.

W naszym zespole badamy zastosowanie podwodnego Gaussian Splattingu do trenowania modeli wizji komputerowej. Z modelu 3D sceny generujemy „sztuczne” zdjęcia, na których robot uczy się rozpoznawać obiekty.

Za tę pracę BlueSpark otrzymał Research Award na RoboSub 2026.

Od kilku zdjęć do danych treningowych

  1. Zdjęciakilkadziesiąt ujęć sceny z basenu
  2. Pozycje kamerCOLMAP sam ustala, skąd zrobiono zdjęcia
  3. Model 3DGaussian Splatting odtwarza scenę razem z wodą
  4. Sztuczne zdjęcianowe ujęcia z automatycznie zaznaczonymi obiektami
  5. Trening AIYOLO na zawody i wykrywanie anomalii
Dla dociekliwych: jak to działa od strony technicznej

Gaussian Splatting to bardzo sprytna metoda rekonstrukcji sceny z pojedynczych zdjęć. Dzięki programowi COLMAP nie potrzebujemy nawet danych o miejscach, z których robiono zdjęcia: na podstawie wspólnych punktów na zdjęciach program sam wyznacza względne pozycje kamer (tzw. camera poses).

Znając te pozycje, algorytm optymalizuje ułożenie gaussianów na scenie: tworzy je lub usuwa i dostosowuje ich parametry tak, aby rendery z tych samych miejsc, z których robiono zdjęcia, jak najbardziej przypominały oryginały.

100×Gaussian Splatting jest często ponad 100 razy szybszy niż wcześniejsze metody, takie jak NeRF. Efektem są bardzo przekonujące modele 3D.

Ponieważ gaussiany mają swoją fizyczną pozycję w przestrzeni, obiekty na scenie można łatwo zaznaczyć, oznaczając należące do nich gaussiany. Dzięki temu pomijamy żmudne ręczne oznaczanie danych na zdjęciach: pozycję szukanego obiektu na sztucznym zdjęciu generujemy automatycznie.

Używamy podwodnego Gaussian Splattingu, który wzbogaca model o reprezentację medium. W naszym przypadku jest to woda, ale może to być też na przykład mgła. Pracujemy nad zastosowaniem tej metody do skutecznego trenowania modeli wizji komputerowej: wykrywania anomalii oraz dotrenowywania modelu YOLO na zawody.
researchHtml.en:
Research

Gaussian Splatting

A remarkable technique that reconstructs entire 3D scenes from just a few photographs.

Our team studies underwater Gaussian Splatting for training computer vision models. We generate synthetic images from a 3D scene, allowing a robot to learn to recognise objects.

This research earned BlueSpark the Research Award at RoboSub 2026.

From photographs to training data

  1. Photosdozens of views of a pool scene
  2. Camera posesCOLMAP automatically estimates where each photo was taken
  3. 3D modelGaussian Splatting reconstructs the scene, including the water
  4. Synthetic imagesnew views with automatically annotated objects
  5. AI trainingYOLO for competitions and anomaly detection
A closer look: the technical details

Gaussian Splatting is an ingenious technique for reconstructing scenes from individual photographs. With COLMAP, we do not even need to know where the photographs were taken: the software estimates the relative camera positions, known as camera poses, from points shared across the images.

Using these poses, the algorithm optimises the Gaussians in the scene: it creates or removes them and adjusts their parameters so that renders from the same viewpoints match the original photographs as closely as possible.

100×Gaussian Splatting is often more than 100 times faster than earlier methods such as NeRF. It produces highly convincing 3D reconstructions.

Because Gaussians have physical positions in space, objects in the scene can be annotated by selecting the Gaussians that belong to them. This removes the need for laborious manual image annotation: the position of an object in a synthetic image is generated automatically.

We use underwater Gaussian Splatting, which extends the model with a representation of the surrounding medium. In our case this is water, but it could also be fog, for example. We are exploring how this technique can improve computer vision training, including anomaly detection and fine-tuning YOLO for competitions.
